synopsis: FAA Advisory Circular 20-146A, dated June 2018, is the booklet’s clearest simulation-as-compliance precedent: a baseline seat undergoes physical dynamic testing and model validation, after which eligible variants within the same family may use simulation; changes to load paths, failure mechanisms, materials or interfaces require new physical evidence [f14654, f14655, f14656, f14657]. Aerospace also accepts satisfactory service history for sufficiently similar systems when differences are identified and justified, but simulation extrapolation remains limited to conditions similar to those physically validated [f14659, f14658]. The transferable rules are that calibration is not validation and agreement with another validated model is insufficient; the seat guidance’s 10% agreement criteria are application-specific and must not become generic off-road braking tolerances [f7625, f7626, f7779]. Validation must address decision-relevant quantities and uncertainty: one FAA example had only 0.3% peak error but 60.4% time-history error, while another required about 1,430 lb to provide 95% confidence below a 1,500 lb limit [f7622, f7555, f7794]. DO-178C concerns airborne software, DO-330 qualifies tools whose outputs are relied upon without further checking but does not establish physics-model validity, and MIL-STD-3022 documents model verification, validation and accreditation; the booklet did not verify these three standards [f14660, f14661, f14662, f14663, f14664]. For the collision-mitigation program, simulator errors can mask defects, so tool qualification should be budgeted separately from establishing model validity [f14669, f14670, f14662].
